title: Stokes’ Theorem
lead: Stokes’ theorem carries Green’s theorem from a plane region to a surface in space: the circulation of a field around the boundary of a surface equals the flux of its curl across the surface. This section states and proves it, uses it to evaluate line and surface integrals each through the other, reads curl as circulation per unit area, and derives Faraday’s law.
objectives: Explain the meaning of Stokes’ theorem.
Use Stokes’ theorem to evaluate a line integral.
Use Stokes’ theorem to calculate a surface integral.
Use Stokes’ theorem to calculate a curl.
summary_html:
• Stokes’ theorem relates a flux integral over a surface to a line integral around the boundary of the surface. Stokes’ theorem is a higher dimensional version of Green’s theorem, and therefore is another version of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in higher dimensions.
  • Stokes’ theorem can be used to transform a difficult surface integral into an easier line integral, or a difficult line integral into an easier surface integral.
  • Through Stokes’ theorem, line integrals can be evaluated using the simplest surface with boundary C.
  • Faraday’s law relates the curl of an electric field to the rate of change of the corresponding magnetic field. Stokes’ theorem can be used to derive Faraday’s law.

footnotes.html: The book prints “flux form”; the equation that follows, $\oint\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\iint\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{N}\,dS,$ is the circulation form of Green’s theorem.

In this example the inner integral’s lower limit is printed $\sqrt{4-x^{2}}$ for $-\sqrt{4-x^{2}},$ and both integrals cite Equation 16.19, the scalar surface integral; the flux integral is computed by Equation 16.21 and the line integral by Equation 16.9. The figure’s caption calls the paraboloid a hemisphere.

The tangent vector is printed $\langle -\sin t,0,\cos t\rangle;$ for $\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle \sin t,0,1-\cos t\rangle$ it is $\langle \cos t,0,\sin t\rangle,$ so the integrand is $\cos t-\cos 2t$ and the integral is again $0.$
The link names Equation 16.19, the scalar surface integral; the flux of $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}$ is computed by Equation 16.21.
By Faraday’s law $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{E}=-\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}=-\langle x,y,-2z\rangle=\langle -x,-y,2z\rangle;$ the key prints it without the minus sign.
Figure 16.83’s caption calls the surface a hemisphere; it is the paraboloid $z=4-x^{2}-y^{2},$ $z\ge 0.$

assumes.text: A small piece of $\kS$ is approximated by an oriented square $E$ with sides $E_{l},$ $E_{d},$ $E_{r}$ and $E_{u},$ which inherits its orientation from $\kS$.
On a flat square, the circulation form of Green’s theorem reads $\int_{\partial E}\kvecF\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\iint_{E}\kcurlF\cdot\kvecN dS$, with $\kvecN$ the unit normal of the square.
The approximating square $F$ to the left of $E$ has the same orientation, and its right side is the left side of $E$ traversed the other way: $E_{l}=-F_{r}$.
Every side of an approximating square that does not approximate the boundary of $\kS$ is shared with an adjacent square, and the same holds for the other three sides of $E$.
As the areas of the approximating squares go to zero, the sum of the fluxes approaches the flux across $\kS$ and the sides along the boundary approach $\kC$.

then.why: Each square’s flux is the line integral around its boundary; add over all the squares.

steps.cap: Each shared side is traversed once in each direction, and the two line integrals cancel; only the sides approximating the boundary of $\kS$ survive.

\mk{L}{\int_{C}\kvecF\cdot d\mathbf{r}}=\iint_{D}\begin{array}{l}\mk{q}{(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y})}\\ -\mk{p}{(\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x})}\end{array}dA
steps.cap: Each component depends on $x$ through $z$ as well, so the chain rule adds a term $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$; the product $R\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ is differentiated by the product rule.

then.tex: \mk{L}{\int_{C}\kvecF\cdot d\mathbf{r}}=\iint_{D}\begin{array}{l}\mk{q}{(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y})}\\ -\mk{p}{(\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial P}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x})}\end{array}dA

steps.cap: With $\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y}=\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x},$ four of the terms appear once with each sign and disappear.

assumes.text: If $D_{r}$ is small enough, $(\kcurlF)(P)\approx(\kcurlF)(P_{0})$ for all points $P$ in $D_{r}$, because the curl is continuous; on the flat disk the unit normal is $\kvecN(P_{0})$ throughout.
The area of the disk $D_{r}$ is $\pi r^{2}$.
The approximation gets arbitrarily close as the radius shrinks to zero.

steps.cap: The quantity $(\kcurlF)(P_{0})\cdot\kvecN(P_{0})$ is constant, so it comes out of the integral, and what is left is the area of the disk.
